title: Boolean Conditions in C
learningObjectives: Explain how C conditions interpret zero as false and nonzero as true.
Use _Bool and the bool, true and false names where supported by the selected C version.
Recognize that relational and logical operators produce int results in C.
Distinguish logical operators && and || from bitwise operators & and |.
Write clear conditions and test boundary cases around zero and nonzero values.

understand.concept: C conditions use scalar expressions: zero is false and nonzero is true. The type _Bool stores the values 0 or 1. The stdbool.h header provides bool, true and false convenience macros in C versions where the header defines them. Relational and logical operators produce int results in C. Logical && and || short-circuit; bitwise & and | operate on integer representations.
understand.whyItMatters: Reliable decisions depend on clear conditions. Explicit boolean intent makes code easier to read and helps avoid confusing numeric values, pointers and truth conditions.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Truth values in C

C does not require a separate built-in Boolean keyword in the way some languages do. In a condition, zero is false and any nonzero scalar value is true. The type `_Bool` stores 0 or 1.

## 2. bool, true and false

In C versions where `<stdbool.h>` provides them as macros, `bool`, `true` and `false` make Boolean intent easier to read. These names do not change the underlying rules for conditions.

## 3. Relational and logical operators

Operators such as `<`, `>=`, `==` and `!=` compare values. Logical `&&` means AND and `||` means OR. Logical `!` negates a truth value. In C, these operators produce an int result of 0 or 1.

## 4. Short-circuit evaluation

For `A && B`, B is evaluated only if A is true. For `A || B`, B is evaluated only if A is false. This lets code safely check a pointer before dereferencing it in the right operand, provided the left condition establishes the required guarantee.

## 5. Logical versus bitwise

`&&` and `||` combine truth conditions and short-circuit. `&` and `|` are bitwise operators on integer operands and do not short-circuit. Use the operator that matches the intended meaning.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small C program that demonstrates the central rules in CL2.10. Compile with warnings enabled, run it with ordinary and boundary values, and explain each result in your own words.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL2.10 using different values and names. Include one likely mistake as a separate experiment, observe the compiler diagnostic or behavior, then correct it. Record the rule that explains the correction.

questions.prompt: How does C interpret a scalar condition?
options: Zero is false and nonzero is true
Only 1 is true; all other values are invalid
questions.answer: Zero is false and nonzero is true
questions.explanation: C conditions use zero for false and nonzero for true.
The _Bool type represents Boolean values as 0 or 1.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between && and &?
options: && is logical and short-circuits; & is bitwise and does not short-circuit
questions.answer: && is logical and short-circuits; & is bitwise and does not short-circuit
questions.explanation: Logical AND can skip evaluation of its right operand.

questions.prompt: When is the right operand of A || B evaluated?
questions.explanation: Logical OR short-circuits when its left operand is true.

questions.prompt: What type do relational and logical operators produce in C?
options: bool as a distinct mandatory keyword type
questions.explanation: These operators produce an int value of zero or one.
